blocks.text: Ezekiel 33 can be read within a book that maintains Ezekiel’s first-person voice while also showing signs of collection, coordination, repetition, and textual development compatible with scribal shaping. This remains debated. A practical outline places chapters 33–39 after chapters 1–3, 4–24, and 25–32, without deciding either the book’s chronology or how it was composed. The report that Jerusalem has fallen fits the book’s narrated horizon, which runs from the 597 deportation through Jerusalem’s siege and destruction and onward to restoration and nation-oracles dated in the 570s BCE.

The chapter’s insistence that each person can turn from wrongdoing and live belongs with the book’s stated rejection of fatalism: responsibility is presented as personal, and neither former righteousness nor former wickedness fixes the outcome when a person’s conduct changes. That context helps explain why the watchman’s warning and the hearer’s response both receive such close attention in Ezekiel 33.

sections.title: Reading the Chapter in the Book
